div.head: VI Atr 42.3
div.ab: ⁊ þæt hy Godes cyrican æghwar georne griðian ⁊ friþian ⁊ mid leohte ⁊ lacum hi gelome gegretan, ⁊ hy sylfe þær georne to Christe gebiddan.
and þæt hi Godes circan æghwar georne griðian ⁊ friðian ⁊ mid leohte ⁊ lacum gelome hig gegretan, ⁊ híg silfe þar georne gebiddan.
⁊ þæt hy Godes cyrican æghwar georne griðian ⁊ friþian ⁊ mid leohte ⁊ lacum hi gelome gegretan ⁊ hy sylfe þær georne to Christe gebiddan.
And þæt hy Godes cyrican æghwar georne griðian and friþian, and mid leohte and lacum hi gelome gegretan, and hy sylfe þær georne to Christe gebiddan.
und dass sie überall Gottes Kirchen gern mit Schutzgewalt und Friedensrecht umgeben und sie oft mit Lichtkerzen und Gaben besuchen und dort selbst eifrig zu Christus beten.
and that they eagerly protect and keep the peace of God's churches everywhere, and often visit them with candles and offerings, and there themselves pray eagerly (to Christ, K).

and that they should diligently maintain the security and sanctity of the churches of God everywhere, and frequently visit them with candles and offerings, and themselves there earnestly pray to Christ.
And they are to everywhere diligently preserve and protect God’s churches, and to visit them frequently with candles and offerings, and there themselves pray fervently to Christ.

note.seg: Dieselbe Mahnung o. 13. Diese Zeilen wiederholt I Cn 2; sie sind aber homiletischer Gemeinplatz. Das Wort griðian (s. d. Wb), vom Nord. Lehnwort grið gebildet, kommt erst seit 11. Jh. vor; mit dem reimenden friðian begegnet es öfter. Wenn ein Bedeutungsunterschied vorliegt, was nicht überall feststeht, so will frið die Sicherheit, genossen gegenüber Angreifern, grið die privilegierte Macht, anderen Sicherheit zu gewähren, ausdrücken; s. Gl Schutz 3a. b; Kirchenfriede Z. 3; n. 1

The same admonition above 13. These lines are repeated by I Cn 2; they are, however, a homiletic commonplace. The word griðian (see that word in Wb), formed from the Norse loanword grið, occurs only from the 11th cent. onwards; it is often found together with the rhyming friðian. If there is a difference in meaning, which is not established in every case, frið is meant to express the security enjoyed against attackers, grið the privileged power to grant security to others; see Gl Schutz 3a. b; Kirchenfriede l. 3; n. 1
Lichtschoss (s. d. Gl 5) wird o. 19 gefordert, hier, wenigstens dem Worte nach, die Kerze in Natura. Dieselbe Zeile in Hom. n. Wulfstan 73
Light-scot (see that word in Gl 5) is demanded above 19; here, at least according to the wording, the candle in kind. The same line in Hom. n. Wulfstan 73

Cf. 13; I Cn. 2.
The verb griðian, derived from the Scandinavian loan word grið, begins to appear in the eleventh century (cf. Sax. Chr. ann. 1016, 1046, 1068 etc.). It is often found along with the rhyming friðian. Liebermann regards the two terms grið and frið as practically synonymous by the time of Æthelred (see ii. p. 642 s.v. Schutz, 3 a), but suggests that if there is any underlying difference between them, frið has the special sense of security against assailants, while grið implies the privilege of assuring safety to others.
